content: 1. Immediate Availability of Support in Healthcare Settings: This recommendation is based on indirect evidence. 2. Training for Healthcare Providers: In-service training and pre-qualification education should be provided to healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, and midwives, to equip them with the skills to offer first-line support to women who have experienced intimate partner violence or sexual assault. 3. Counseling for Pregnant Women Experiencing Violence: Pregnant women who disclose intimate partner violence should be offered empowerment counseling (up to 12 sessions) and advocacy/support services, including safety planning, provided by trained professionals. However, the feasibility of implementing this in settings outside antenatal care or in lowand middle-income countries remains uncertain. 4. Integration of Services: Care for women experiencing intimate partner violence and sexual assault should be integrated into existing health services rather than being offered as standalone services. 5. Mandatory Reporting Not Recommended: Healthcare providers are not recommended to engage in mandatory reporting of intimate partner violence to law enforcement authorities. 6. HIV and Tuberculosis (TB) Treatment for Healthcare Workers: Free HIV and TB treatment should be provided to healthcare workers in a non-stigmatizing, gender-sensitive, confidential, and convenient setting, especially when their facility does not offer antiretroviral therapy (ART) or when they prefer off-site services. 7. Policies to Prevent Discrimination: Policies should be introduced or reinforced to prevent discrimination against healthcare workers living with HIV or TB. Interventions to reduce stigma among colleagues and supervisors are also recommended. 8. Sexuality-Related Communication: Brief sexuality-related communication (BSC) is recommended for the prevention of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among adults and adolescents in primary healthcare settings. 9. Adolescents should be counseled on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status and supported in making informed decisions about if, when, how, and to whom to disclose. 10. Initiatives should be implemented to enforce privacy protections and establish policies, laws, and norms that prevent discrimination and promote acceptance of people living with HIV. 11. In countries where HIV transmission occurs among serodiscordant couples, daily oral PrEP (e.g., tenofovir or tenofovir/emtricitabine) may be considered as an additional prevention option for the uninfected partner. 12. Contraceptive Use for Women with HIV: Women living with asymptomatic or mild HIV (WHO stage 1 or 2) can use various hormonal contraceptive methods without restriction, including combined oral contraceptives (COCs), combined injectable contraceptives (CICs), contraceptive patches and rings, progestogen-only pills (POPs), progestogen-only injectables (POIs), and implants. Women with severe or advanced HIV (WHO stage 3 or 4) should generally not initiate the use of levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices (LNG-IUDs) until their condition improves to asymptomatic or mild HIV. However, women already using LNG-IUDs do not need to have them removed but should be closely monitored for pelvic infections. 13. ART for Adolescents and Pregnant Women: ART should be initiated in all adolescents and pregnant or breastfeeding women living with HIV, regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count, and continued lifelong. 14. Breastfeeding Recommendations: Mothers living with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue for up to 24 months or longer while being fully supported for ART adherence. Mixed feeding is not a reason to stop breastfeeding if ART is being used. 15. Safe Abortion Services: Women living with HIV who seek voluntary abortion should have access to the same safe abortion services as all other women. 16. HPV Vaccination: The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine is recommended for girls aged 9–13 years. Girls receiving their first dose before age 15 can follow a two-dose schedule with a six-month interval. Immunocompromised individuals, including those living with HIV, and females aged 15 years and older should receive three doses for full protection. 17. Addressing Violence Against Key Populations: Violence against key populations, including women living with HIV, should be prevented and addressed in partnership with organizations led by these populations. Comprehensive post-rape care should be provided in accordance with WHO guidelines. 18. Training for Law Enforcement and Healthcare Providers: Law enforcement officials and healthcare providers should be trained to recognize and uphold the human rights of key populations and held accountable for any violations, including acts of violence. 19. Legal and Policy Reforms: Countries should work towards decriminalizing behaviors such as drug use, sex work, and same-sex activity, as well as eliminating unjust applications of civil laws against marginalized groups. Legal recognition of transgender individuals and their preferred gender and name is also encouraged to reduce stigma and improve access to HIV services. 20. Contraceptive Access for Adolescents: Contraceptives should be made affordable and accessible to all, including adolescents, without requiring mandatory parental or guardian authorization. 21. Empowering Women Living with HIV: Women living with HIV should be empowered and engaged in the development of policies and programs that affect them. Comprehensive assessments of food security and access to tailored sexual and reproductive health services should be integral to their care. 22. Global Guidance and Adaptation: These guidelines are intended to support healthcare providers, program managers, and policymakers globally. They should be adapted to local contexts, taking into account the HIV epidemic, economic conditions, and existing healthcare services. 23. Focus on Women Living with HIV: Women living with HIV face unique challenges and rights violations related to their gender, sexuality, and reproductive roles. Addressing these issues is critical to ensuring their sexual and reproductive health and rights. These recommendations aim to create an enabling environment for women living with HIV, improve access to healthcare, and promote gender equality and human rights.
